sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte latin de zoo77/1l.xml (edition Carmody 1941, Physiologus Latinus Versio Y), deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. 49 chapitres correspondant exactement au decoupage du temoin latin (memes xml:id).

div.head: On the Lion
div.p: We begin to speak first of the lion, king of all beasts.
Jacob, blessing his son Judah, said: 'Judah's whelp is a lion's cub.'
The Physiologus, who wrote of the natures of these matters, said the lion has three natures.

The first nature is this: when it walks scenting on the mountain, the smell of the hunter comes to it; and with its tail it covers its tracks wherever it goes, so that the hunter may not follow its tracks and find its lair and capture it.

So too our Savior, the spiritual lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, sent by the co-eternal Father, covered his intelligible tracks (that is, his divinity) from the unbelieving Jews: with angels an angel, with archangels an archangel, with thrones a throne, with power a power -- until, descending, he had come down into the womb of the virgin, to save mankind, which had perished: 'And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.' And this, not knowing him as he descended and ascended, those who are above say: 'Who is this king of glory?' and the angels leading him answered: 'The Lord of hosts, he is the king of glory.'
The second nature of the lion is: when it sleeps, its eyes keep watch, for they are open.

In the Song of Songs the bridegroom testifies, saying: 'I sleep, but my heart watches.' For indeed my Lord slept bodily on the cross, but his divinity ever watches at the right hand of the Father: 'He who keeps Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.'
When the lioness gives birth to her cub, she bears it dead; and the lioness guards it for three days, until its father comes on the third day and, breathing upon its face, rouses it.
So the almighty Father of all raised on the third day the firstborn of all creation from the dead. Well then did Jacob say: 'Judah's whelp is a lion's cub -- who shall rouse him?'

div.head: On the Antelope
div.p: There is an animal called the antelope, exceedingly fierce, so that not even the hunter can approach it. It has long horns shaped like a saw, so that it can cut down great and tall trees, and bring them to the ground. If it grows thirsty, it goes to the terrible river Euphrates and drinks; and there are there certain bushes called 'ricinae' in Greek, that is, shrubs with slender branches; and it comes playing to that ricinus bush, and is caught fast in its branches. And it cries out, wishing to flee, and cannot, for it is bound; and the hunter, hearing it, comes and kills it.

O citizen of heaven -- that is, one whose way of life is heavenly -- presuming upon your two horns, abstain from detraction and from pleasures, from opposing desire and from the pomp of this world: the powers of the angels rejoice with you; the two horns are the two Testaments. But take care lest you be caught by this ricinus, that is, by the tiny shrub through which occasion clothes you and you are held fast by its snares, and the evil hunter -- that is, the devil -- kill you: 'Wine and women the wise man shall flee.'

div.head: On the Fire-Stones
div.p: There are certain stones called pyroboli only in the regions of the East -- that is, fiery stones, male and female. And as long as they are far from one another, the fire does not burn; but if the male comes near the female, the fire is kindled and burns up everything.
O noble citizen of heaven -- that is, one abstinent in all things -- for many are in hell on account of woman, who fell into temptations.

div.head: On the Sea-Saw
div.p: The Physiologus spoke well of those who abstain in all things but do not persevere to the end.

There is, he says, an animal in the sea called the saw-fish, having long wings. And if it sees ships sailing, it imitates them, and raises up its wings, and contends with the sailing ships; and when it has gone thirty or forty furlongs, or more, wearying itself, it folds its wings, and the waves carry it back to its old place, where it was before.

The sea is said to be this world; the ships are the prophets and apostles who passed through this world; and the powers of the Adversary -- this saw-fish, which did not remain with the passing ships -- are the likeness of those who abstain for a time, and, running the good race, did not persevere -- beginning a good work, they did not persevere to the end, on account of covetousness and pride and shameful gain, or fornications or adulteries or hatred: in these waves of the sea -- that is, the contrary powers -- are those who lead them down to hell.

div.head: On the Charadrius
div.p: There is another kind of flying animal called the charadrius: it is written of in Deuteronomy. It is entirely white, having no black part; and its inward parts, applied as a poultice, cure those whose eyes are dim. It is found in the courts of kings. And if anyone is sick, it is known from this same charadrius whether he will live or die; and if the man's sickness is unto death, the charadrius turns its face away from him, and all know that he will die; but if his sickness is unto life, the charadrius looks upon the face of the sick man, and the sick man upon the charadrius, and the charadrius draws out the sickness of the sick man; and flying up into the sun's air, it burns away the sickness of the sick man, and scatters it.

Our Savior too is the charadrius, and he who is sick takes on the good likeness of our Savior: for the Savior is entirely white, having no spot or wrinkle; for the Lord himself says in the Gospel: 'The prince of this world will come and find nothing in me'; and indeed: 'He did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.' For coming down from heaven to the people of the Jews, he turned his divinity away from them, saying: 'Behold, your house is left to you desolate'; he came to us the Gentiles, taking away our infirmities, and bearing our sins, lifted up on the wood of the cross: 'Ascending on high, he led captivity captive, he gave gifts to men.'

But you say that the charadrius is unclean according to the law, and how does it bear the likeness of the Savior? The serpent too is unclean, and the Lord himself testified of himself in the Gospel, saying: 'As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up'; and the serpent is called more prudent; likewise also of the lion, and many other things: for creatures are twofold, both praiseworthy and blameworthy.

div.head: On the Pelican
div.p: David says in the hundred and first psalm: 'I have become like the pelican in the wilderness.'

The Physiologus says of the pelican that it is exceedingly fond of its young; and if it has begotten offspring and the little ones have grown, they begin to strike their parents in the face; but the parents, striking back, kill them; then, moved by mercy, the parents weep for them three days, mourning those they have killed; and on the third day their mother, striking her own side, lets her blood drip down upon their dead bodies -- that is, of the chicks: and this very blood raises them up from death.

So too our Lord rebukes through Isaiah, saying: 'I have begotten and raised up sons, but they have despised me.' The maker of all creation begot us: we struck him. How did we strike him? Because we served the creature rather than the Creator. But ascending to the height of the cross, the wicked struck his side and opened his rib; and there came out blood and water unto eternal life -- blood, because of which it is said: 'Taking the cup, he gave thanks'; water, because of the baptism of repentance -- he who said: 'They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water,' and so on.
Well then did the Physiologus speak of the pelican.

div.head: On the Night-Raven
div.p: Likewise in the same hundred and first psalm it says of the night-raven: 'I have become like a night-raven in the house.'
The night-raven loves darkness more than light; it is a kind of flying creature.

Our Lord Jesus Christ loved those who were in darkness and the shadow of death -- the people of the Gentiles and the people of the Jews -- who then had the adoption of sons and the promise of the fathers. Of this the Savior also said: 'Fear not, little flock, for it has pleased the Father to give you the kingdom'; and the prophet says: 'I will call those not my people, my beloved.'

But you say (according to Deuteronomy) that the night-raven is an unclean bird: and the Apostle therefore said: 'He who knew no sin became sin for us'; and: 'He was made all things to all men, that he might gain all.'

div.head: On the Eagle
div.p: David in the hundred and second psalm: 'Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's.'

The Physiologus says of the eagle that when it grows old, its wings grow heavy, and its eyes grow dim. What then does it do? It seeks a spring of water, and flies up into the sun's air, and burns off its wings and the dimness of its eyes; and it comes down into the spring, and dips itself three times, and is renewed and made new.

So then you too, if you have an old garment, and the eyes of your heart grow dim, seek the spiritual fountain, the Lord: what is meant: 'They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water,' and so on. And flying up into the height of the sun of righteousness, who is Christ Jesus (as the Apostle says), he will burn away your old garment of the devil. For this reason those two elders in Daniel heard themselves called 'grown old in evil days,' and were told to be baptized in the everlasting fountain, stripping off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new, 'who is created according to the Lord,' as the Apostle says. For this reason David said: 'Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's.'

div.head: On the Phoenix
div.p: Because the Savior said in the Gospel: 'I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again': and the Jews were angered at his word.

There is a kind of flying creature in the regions of India called the phoenix; this bird, every five hundred years, enters into the trees of Lebanon and fills both its wings with spices. And it makes this known to the priest of Heliopolis (this is a city having the name Heliopolis) in the month of new things, that is Adar, which in Greek is called Pharmuthi or Phamenoth. And the priest, when this has been made known to him, enters and fills the altar with vine-shoot wood; and that bird, entering Heliopolis laden with spices, mounts upon the altar, and kindles a fire for itself, and burns itself up. And on the next day the priest examines the altar, and finds a worm in the ashes. On the second day he finds a tiny little bird. On the third day he finds a great eagle: and flying up, it salutes the priest, and goes to its ancient place.

If then this kind of flying creature has such power to kill itself thus and to raise itself up thus, how do foolish men grow angry at the word of the Savior, who says: 'I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again'? The phoenix takes on the person of the Savior: for descending from the heavenly places, he laid down his two wings full of his good fragrance (that is, his excellent words): that we too, stretching out the works of our hands, might send back to him a good spiritual fragrance in good works.
Well then did the Physiologus speak of the phoenix.

div.head: On the Hoopoe
div.p: For the law says: 'Whoever curses father or mother shall surely die.' And how are there those who kill father or mother?

There is a bird called the hoopoe: if it sees that its parents have grown old, and their eyes have grown dim, the young ones pluck the feathers of their parents, and lick their eyes, and warm their parents under their own wings, and nourish their parents, repaying them, and feed them as their own chicks, and their parents are made new; and in a manner they say to their parents: as you labored, nourishing us, so we too do the same for you.
And how do unreasoning men not love their parents?
Well then did the Physiologus argue concerning the hoopoe.

div.head: On the Wild Ass
div.p: It is said in Job: 'Who is it that lets the wild ass go free?'
The Physiologus says of the wild ass that it is the leader of its herd; and if it begets young males, their father breaks their organs, so that they cannot beget seed.

The patriarchs sought to create carnal seed; the apostles, however, gained spiritual sons from fleshly ones, so that they might possess heavenly seed, as it says: 'Rejoice, barren one, who bears not,' and so on. The Old Testament announces seed, but the New preaches abstinence.

div.head: On the Viper
div.p: John says to the Pharisees: 'Brood of vipers.'

The Physiologus says of the viper that the male has the face of a man; the female, however, has the face of a woman as far as the navel, but from the navel to the tail she has the shape of a crocodile; moreover the female has no hidden place, that is, no member for giving birth, but only what is like the eye of a needle. If the male mates with the female, he pours his seed into the female's mouth; and if she drinks his seed, the female bites off the male's organs -- that is, his virile parts -- and the male dies; but when her young have grown in their mother's womb, since she has no opening through which to give birth, then the young ones tear open their mother's side, and come out, killing their mother.

Our Savior therefore likened the Pharisees to the viper: as this brood kills father and mother, so too this people, who are without God, killed their father Jesus Christ and their earthly mother Jerusalem. And how shall they flee from the wrath to come? But our Father Jesus Christ and our Mother the Church live forever, while they, living in sin, are dead.

div.head: On the Serpent
div.p: The Savior says: 'Be wise as serpents, and gentle as doves.'
The serpent has three natures.

Its first nature is this: when it grows old, its eyes grow dim; and if it wishes to become new, it abstains and fasts forty days, until its skin is loosened from its flesh; and when its skin has been loosened by fasting, it goes seeking a narrow crevice in a rock, and enters into the crevice, and rubs itself, and forces itself through, and casts off its old skin, and becomes new.

And we too, through much abstinence and affliction, for Christ's sake, cast off the old man and his garment. But you too, seek the spiritual rock, Christ, and the narrow crevice: for narrow is the gate, and the way that leads to life is one of affliction, and there are few who enter by it.
Its second nature is: when it comes to drink water at the river, it does not bring with it the venom it carries in its head, but leaves it in its den.

So too we, when we come into the assembly, ought to draw living and everlasting water; when we hear the divine and heavenly word in church, let us not bring venom in with us -- that is, earthly and evil desires. For many foolish ones did not come to that spiritual supper; some buying five yoke of oxen, others seeking a field, others taking a wife. As it says in the Gospel: 'Render therefore to all their dues; fear to whom fear is due, honor to whom honor is due, tribute to whom tribute is due,' and so on.
Its third nature is: if it sees a man naked, it fears him; but if it sees him clothed, it leaps upon him.

So too we understand this spiritually: that when our first father Adam was naked in paradise, the serpent could not prevail to leap upon him; but when he was clothed in a tunic -- that is, the mortality of the fleshly body of sin -- then it leapt upon him. So if you too have a mortal garment, that is, the old man, and wish to hear yourself called 'grown old in evil days,' the serpent will leap upon you; but if you strip yourself of the garment of the rulers and powers of this world and of the spirits of wickedness in the heavens (as the Apostle said), then the serpent cannot leap upon you.

div.head: On the Ant
div.p: Solomon in the Proverbs said: 'Go to the ant, O sluggard, and imitate its ways.'
The Physiologus said the ant has three natures.

Its first nature is this: when they walk in order, each one carries a grain in its mouth; those that are empty, having nothing, do not say to those that have, 'give us your grain'; but they go along the tracks of those before them, and come to the place where the others found grain; and taking some themselves too, they carry it to their own dwelling.

These things indeed were said of the foolish and unreasoning. But woe to those virgins who asked of the wise, saying: 'Give us oil from your vessels, for our lamps are going out'; though they were reasonable and had understanding, they heard this: 'We cannot, lest perhaps there not be enough for us and for you.'
Its second nature is: when it stores grain in its dwelling, it divides it in two, lest perhaps winter come upon it, and the rain falling on it cause the grain to sprout, and it perish of hunger.

And you, divide the fleshly words of the Old Testament from the spiritual word, lest the letter should sprout and kill you. For the apostle Paul says that the law is spiritual; and again he says: 'The letter kills, but the spirit gives life'; and again: 'What things give life -- these are the two Testaments.' The Jews, however, looking only at the letter, were killed by hunger; and they became murderers of the prophets, and indeed of God, shaving the rods so that the sheep might give birth, and fleshly circumcisions, and sabbaths, and the feast of tabernacles. But all these things are spiritual and intelligible.

Its third nature is: it goes into the field at harvest time, and climbs up the ear of grain, and takes down a grain. But before it climbs the ear, it smells beneath the ear, and by the smell knows whether it is wheat or barley; and if it is barley, it flees at once to an ear of wheat. Barley is the food of cattle; and it says in Job: 'Let barley grow for me instead of wheat.'

And the prophet: 'Flee from Babylon, flee from the land of the Chaldeans' -- that is, flee foreign doctrine of foreign glory, which is the food of barley, killing souls (these things are said, and are, hostile to the truth).

div.head: On the Siren and the Onocentaur
div.p: The prophet Isaiah signified this beforehand, saying: 'Sirens and onocentaurs and demons and hedgehogs shall come into Babylon and dance.'

The Physiologus discussed the nature of each, saying of the sirens, that they are deadly creatures in the sea, crying out with strange voices; for down to the navel they have the shape of a man, but below that, of a bird. Likewise the onocentaurs, from the chest upward have the shape of a man, but below, of a donkey.

So too is the man of a double heart, unstable in all his ways. Such are evil traders, and the deeds of the soul; in church indeed they gather, but secretly they sin: having, as the Apostle said, a form of godliness but denying its power. And in the church the souls of some are like sheep; but when they are dismissed from the assembly, they become like cattle: 'they are compared to senseless beasts.' Such as these, whether sirens or onocentaurs, show the likeness of adversaries.

div.head: On the Hedgehog
div.p: The hedgehog does not have an appearance like other animals, but is entirely covered with spines. The Physiologus said of it that it climbs up a cluster of grapes on the vine, and knocks the grapes down to the ground -- that is, the fruit; and rolling itself over them, with the fruit of the vine clinging to its spines, it carries it to its young, and leaves the cluster of grapes empty.

And you, Christian, abstaining from working in all things, for you have stood by the spiritual vine, on whose account you are brought to the spiritual winepress, and are stored up in the courts of God the king, at the holy tribunal of Christ, and shall receive eternal life -- how have you let that most wicked spirit climb up into your place, and scatter such abstinence of yours? And it deceived you with the stings of death, to such a degree that it divided your spoils among the adverse powers.
Well then did the Physiologus set the natures of animals against spiritual matters.

div.head: On the Ibis
div.p: There is an animal called the ibis; it is unclean, according to the law, above all birds. It cannot swim, but feeds along the shore of rivers or pools: it cannot swim in the deep, but only where the unclean little fish stay; it is found outside the deepest places.

Learn now to swim spiritually, that you may come into the intelligible and spiritual deep river, and to the height of the wisdom of the power of God. If you wish to ascend to the height, and to learn the mysteries of the Lord Jesus Christ, learn to swim spiritually. For unless you stretch out both hands and make the form of the cross, you cannot cross the sea; and unless you wish to cross this world to God through the form of the cross, you will not avoid all stumbling blocks: for those who do not know how to swim or to pray feed outside the church. Outside the faith are fornications, adulteries, detractions, covetousness. For the root of all evils is covetousness: indeed the form of the cross is over all creation. And the sun, unless it extends its rays, cannot shine. And the moon, if it does not extend its two horns, will not give light. For the birds of heaven too, unless they extend their wings, cannot fly. The ship likewise, unless its sail is stretched when it sails, is not moved to sail by the blowing winds. So too Moses, stretching out his hands, killed Amalek; Daniel, praying, escaped the lions; Jonah in the belly of the whale was likewise saved by praying; Thecla was thrown into fire, and into the pits of beasts, and the form of the cross saved her. And Susanna was freed from the elders; Judith thus slew Holofernes with her strong right hand; Esther saved her people from Haman; and the three youths in the furnace of fire: by such a sign they were kept safe, and many other saints too suffered the worst of every kind of torment.
Well then did the Physiologus speak of the ibis.

div.head: On the Fox
div.p: The fox is a wholly deceitful animal, and prepares tricks. If it is hungry and finds nothing to eat, it seeks out a place where the earth is cracked and covered with chaff, and throws itself down on its back, looking upward, and draws its breath in beneath it: it stretches itself out entirely. And the birds think it is dead; they come down upon it to eat it, and it seizes them, and stretches out, and the birds die a bad death.

The devil too is wholly dead, and so is the work of his deeds: whoever wishes to share in his flesh will die; for his flesh is fornications, covetousness, pleasures, opposed to the world. Because of this Herod too was likened to the fox; and the scribe, hearing the Savior, said: 'Foxes have holes.' And in the Song of Songs: 'Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards.' And David in the sixty-third psalm: 'They shall be the portion of foxes.'
Well then did the Physiologus speak of the fox.

div.head: On the Peridexion Tree and the Doves
div.p: There is a tree called the peridexion, found in India. The fruit of that tree is entirely and exceedingly sweet, and pleasant. Doves delight in the fruit of that tree: they dwell in it, feeding on its fruit. The dragon is an enemy to doves, and fears that tree and its shadow, in which the doves dwell: and the dragon cannot come near the doves nor its shadow. For if the shadow of the tree falls to the west, the dragon flees to the east; if the shadow again falls to the east, it flees to the west. But if it happens that a dove is found outside the tree or its shadow, and the dragon finds it, it kills it.

The tree is said to be the Father of all, and the shadow the Son, Christ; as Gabriel said to Mary: 'Fear not, Mary, the Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.' The fruit is said to be heavenly wisdom, and the dove is said to be the Holy Spirit; take heed then, O man, lest, after you have received the Holy Spirit (that is, the spiritual and intelligible dove, descending from heaven and remaining upon you), you fall away outside the divinity, estranged from Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and the dragon destroy you (that is, the devil). For the dragon cannot come near the tree, nor its shadow, nor the fruit of the tree: and you, if you have the Holy Spirit, the dragon cannot come near you either (that is, the devil).
Well then have we spoken of the tree and its fruit and its shadow.

div.head: On the Elephant
div.p: There is an animal called the elephant. In it there is no lustful desire for coupling. The tragelaphus, however, is different. If it wishes to beget young, it goes eastward, near paradise; and there is a tree there called the mandrake; and it goes there with its mate, who first takes from the tree, and gives it to her husband, and entices him until he eats. And when the male has eaten, the female at once conceives in her womb. And when the time comes for her to give birth, she goes out into a pool of water; and the water comes up to her udders (that is, the female's), and she lets down her offspring (that is, her young); she lets it down in the waters and the calf swims because it is newborn; and it comes to her thighs, and is nourished from its mother's udders. The elephant guards her as she gives birth, because of the serpent, for the serpent is an enemy to the elephant. If it finds a serpent, it kills it and tramples it, until it dies.

This is its nature: if it falls, it cannot rise. How does it fall, since it leans against a tree? For it has no joints in its knees so as to lie down, if it wished; but the hunter, who wishes to hunt it, cuts through the tree, a little short of all the way, where it is accustomed to lean; so that when the elephant comes and leans upon it, the tree falls, and the animal with it, and they fall together. The elephant cries out: at once a great elephant comes from there, and cannot lift it up; again they both cry out, and twelve other elephants come, and they too cannot lift up the one that has fallen; then they all cry out again, and at once a small elephant comes, and puts its mouth, its trunk, beneath the great one, and lifts it up.
The small elephant has this nature: wherever something is burned from its hair or its bones, neither dragon nor any evil thing befalls there.

The great elephant and his mate take on the persons of Adam and Eve. While they were in virtue (that is, pleasing to the Lord), before their transgression, they did not know coupling, nor did they have understanding of the mixing of their flesh; but when the woman ate of the tree (that is, the intelligible mandrake), and then gave it to her husband, she became pregnant with evils; for which reason they went out of paradise. As long as they were in paradise, Adam did not know her: this is clear, for it is thus written: 'And after Adam and Eve were cast out of paradise,' then Adam knew his wife, and conceiving she bore Cain, above the blameworthy waters: as David said: 'Save me, for the waters have come in even unto my soul.' At once the dragon overthrew them, and made them strangers to virtue (that is, to pleasing God).

And they cried out, crying aloud to the Lord, and the great elephant came (that is, the law), and did not lift him up: just as the priest did not lift up him who fell among thieves. Nor did the twelve elephants lift him up (that is, the choir of prophets), just as the Levite did not lift up him who was wounded by robbers; but the holy intelligible elephant (that is, the Lord Jesus Christ): and though he is greater than all, he became the least of all: for he humbled himself, being made obedient unto death, that he might lift up man, the intelligible Samaritan, who placed us upon his own beast of burden (that is, upon his own body): for he bore our infirmities, and carried our weaknesses. This Samaritan is interpreted in Hebrew as 'guardian'; of whom David says in the hundred and thirteenth psalm: 'The Lord keeps the little ones.'
For where my Lord is present, neither dragon nor any evil can come near.
Well then did the Physiologus speak of the elephant.

div.head: On the Dorcas
div.p: There is an animal in the mountains called dorcas in Greek, caprea in Latin. It loves very high mountains, but finds its food on the lower slopes of the mountains. And it sees from afar all who come to it, and knows whether they come with guile or with friendship.

The caprea has the wisdom of God: it loves the prophets, that is, the high mountains, on which the prophet lifted up his eyes: 'I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence shall come my help.' And Solomon in the Song of Songs said of the dorcas (that is, of the caprea): 'Behold, my beloved leaps upon the mountains, bounding over the hills.' This dorcas leaps upon the prophets, bounding over the hills (that is, the apostles). The dorcas is of sharp sight, signifying that the Savior sees all that is done; he is called God because he sees all things, even from afar, those who come to him with guile; he knew Judas coming to betray him with a kiss; and again it is written: 'The Lord knows them that are his'; and John said: 'Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world.'

div.head: On the Agate Stone, the Sostoros Stone, and the Pearl
div.p: There is a stone called the agate: craftsmen seeking pearls find them by means of this agate stone; divers tie the agate stone to a very strong cord, and lower it into the sea; and the agate stone, coming to the pearl, stops and does not move; at once the divers, following the cord, find the pearl. I shall now tell how the pearl is born: there is a stone in the sea called sostoros; and it comes up from the sea in the early morning before dawn; and it opens its shells (that is, its mouth), and swallows the heavenly dew, and the ray of the sun and moon and the stars above; and so the pearl is born from those things above.

So now this agate stone -- as John himself showed us -- is the intelligible pearl, our Lord Jesus Christ, saying: 'Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world.' The sea is said to be this world, and the divers who bring up the pearl are the choir of the holy teachers; sinners, however, carry it downward, on account of their own wickedness, as far as it concerns them; and the middle of the shell, or of the two wings (that is, it is found in an intelligible sense), is my Lord and Savior (that is, in the middle of the Old and the New Testament), having food from above. My Lord said: 'My kingdom is not of this world,' but from the eternal Father and his holy powers.
Well then did the Physiologus speak of the agate and the pearl.

div.head: On the Adamant Stone
div.p: There is another nature of the adamant stone: it fears neither iron, nor does it receive the smell of smoke; and if it is found in a house, no demon comes near there, nor anything evil; it is found in the houses of kings. Whoever holds it overcomes every man and beast.
The adamant stone is my Lord: if you have him, no evil befalls you.

div.head: On Another Nature of the Wild Ass and the Ape
div.p: There is another nature of the wild ass (the wise man said) that it is found in royal houses: on the twenty-fifth of the month Phamenoth, they know from the wild ass that the day becomes equal to the night: if it cries out twelve times, the king and the palace know that the equality of day comes about (called 'isemeria' in Greek). And the ape, if it urinates seven times, this is the equinox.

The wild ass is the devil, since night (that is, the people of the Gentiles) was made equal to God: the wild ass -- the devil -- cried out to the believing prophets. And the ape has taken on this very person of the devil: it had a beginning, but has no end (that is, no tail); in the beginning he was one of the archangels, but his end is nowhere to be found. And rightly the ape, having no tail, is without form; and shameful is what has no tail -- just as the devil too has no good end.
Well then did the Physiologus speak.

div.head: On the Indian Stone
div.p: There is a stone called the Indian stone, having this nature: if some man has dropsy, skilled physicians seek out this stone. And if they find it, they bind it to the man with dropsy for three hours, and all the foulness will come out of him, the stone drinking it into itself; and when they release the same stone from the man with dropsy, they weigh the stone against the man; and the tiny stone brings the man's body up in the balance -- that is, in weight. But if the stone is left in the sun for three hours, it pours out the foulest water, which it had taken from the body of the man with dropsy, and the stone becomes clean again, as it was before.

The stone is our Lord Jesus Christ. Since we had dropsy, having the waters of the devil in our heart, the stone of the Savior descended and was bound about our heart, his love; but rising from the dead, he took away every intelligible infirmity of our soul: 'And he himself bore our infirmities.'

div.head: On the Herodius, that is the Coot
div.p: There is a flying creature called the herodius, of which David made mention, saying: 'The house of the herodius is their leader' (that is, of the coot, in the hundred and third psalm).

This creature is exceedingly prudent above all birds; it does not seek many dwellings, but where it stays, there too it feeds, and returns there and sleeps; it does not eat carrion, nor does it fly to many places: its dwelling and its food are in one place.

O you too, man of many wanderings, let there be for you one nurse, the everlasting Catholic Church, so that spiritual food and heavenly bread may be digestible in you: do not seek the many places of a foreign glory (that is, of the heretics).

div.head: On the Sycamore
div.p: Amos said: 'I am not a prophet, nor the son of a prophet, but a herdsman, a keeper of goats, plucking sycamore fruit': a herdsman of goats, and he feeds he-goats. Well did Amos take on the person of Christ the Savior. As for what is said, plucking the sycamore fruit: it is an intelligible and spiritual word; and Zacchaeus climbed up into a sycamore tree.

As for what he said, plucking or hollowing out the sycamore fruit for the saints: because before the sycamore fruit is hollowed out, there are within it gnats, that is, dwelling within it in darkness, not seeing the light, saying among themselves: 'We dwell in a great region,' but they are sitting in darkness. But when the sycamore fruit is opened with iron, and they come out from it, they see the brightness of the shining sun, and of the moon and stars, and say: 'We were sitting in darkness, in the shadow' -- of these Isaiah too spoke, saying: 'That he might bring out the bound from their chains, and those dwelling in darkness from the house of prison' -- plucked on the first day, but on the third day the fruit will be made ripe, and will become food for men.

The side of my Savior was pierced, that is, opened by the spear and the iron; and there came out blood and water. But on the third day, rising from the dead, we saw intelligible and spiritual lights: just as the gnats too (that is, the mosquitoes), opening the sycamore fruit, saw the immortal lights. The kids take on the person of those doing penance: for their hair is turned into sackcloth, and they do penance in ashes. The people who sat in darkness saw a great light, and to those who were in the shadow of death, light has arisen. When the sycamore fruit has been opened, on the third day it will become food: our Lord, having been struck, and rising on the third day from the dead, became food and life for us all.

div.head: On the Panther
div.p: The prophet says: 'I have become like a lion to the house of Judah, and like a panther to the house of Ephraim.'

The panther has this nature: it is a friend to all animals, but an enemy to the dragon; it is entirely varied in color, like Joseph's coat, and beautiful. Indeed David said in the forty-fourth psalm: 'The queen stood at your right hand, in a garment of gold, arrayed in varied colors.' The panther is a peaceful animal, and exceedingly gentle. When it has eaten and is full, it immediately sleeps in its den, and on the third day it rises from sleep (so too our Savior). And when the panther rises from sleep on the third day, it cries out with a great voice, and from its voice comes every good fragrance of spices; and those who are far off and those who are near, hearing its voice, follow after the good fragrance of its voice.

Our Lord and Savior, rising from the dead, became a good fragrance to us all, to those far off and those near, peace, as the apostle Paul said: 'the manifold wisdom of God' -- that is, virginity, abstinence, mercy, faith, love, unanimity, peace, joy, patience. In every kind of love the heavenly wisdom of Christ, the God, is varied;

well was it said of the panther, that it is an enemy to the dragon in the water. Nothing then did the divine Scriptures say of flying and living creatures without intelligible purpose; for the Apostle said of Satan: 'We are not ignorant of his devices,' he walks in every way that is not good.

div.head: On the Whale, that is the Aspidochelone
div.p: The Physiologus spoke of a certain whale that is in the sea, called by the name aspidochelone,

exceedingly great, like an island, and heavier than sand, having the shape of the devil. Sailors, not knowing it, tie their ships to it as to an island, and fix their anchors and stakes into it; and they light a fire upon it to cook something for themselves; but if the whale grows hot, it dives, going down into the deep, and sinks all the ships.
So too you, O man, if you hang and bind yourself to the hope of the devil, he sinks you together with himself into the fire of hell.

The whale has another natural trait: if it grows hungry, it opens its mouth wide, and every good smell comes forth from its mouth; and the small fish, smelling this, follow after its scent, and gather themselves in the mouth of that great whale; and when its mouth is full, it closes its mouth, and swallows all those small fish,

that is, those small in faith. But we do not find the greater and perfect fish drawing near to the whale: for the perfect are complete; indeed the apostle Paul said: 'We are not ignorant of his devices.' Job is the most perfect fish, Moses and the other prophets; Joseph escaped the great whale, the wife of the chief of the cooks, as is written in Genesis; likewise Thecla escaped Thamyris, as Susanna escaped the two wicked Babylonian elders; Esther and Judith escaped Ahasuerus and Holofernes; the three youths escaped king Nebuchadnezzar, the great whale; and Sarah, daughter of Raguel, escaped Asmodeus (as in Tobit).

div.head: On the Partridge
div.p: Jeremiah said of the partridge: 'The partridge has cried out, gathering what it did not hatch.'
The partridge warms the eggs of others, laboring and nourishing them; but if the chicks grow, and begin to fly, each one, flying off, flees to its own true parents, and leaves her alone.

So too the devil catches the race of little ones; but when they come to the measure of age, they come to Christ and to the Church, and he is found a fool; today, if someone is of evil habits, tomorrow he may become sober; and you have fled the devil, that is, the partridge, and shall come to your true parents, the just, and the prophets and apostles.

div.head: On the Vulture
div.p: The Physiologus said of the vulture that it is found in high and lofty places; and it sleeps on high rocks and on the pinnacles of temples. If it becomes pregnant, it goes to India, and takes the eutocia-stone: this stone is like snow in size; if you shake it, or someone else grasps it, something within it moves, like a little bell, when it is shaken. And if the pains of birth seize the vulture, it sits upon this stone called eutocia, and gives birth without pain.

And you too, O man, if your soul becomes pregnant with the evil sorrows of the adversary, the devil, take the intelligible inner stone, eutocia. Its outer part is the Mother of God; Mary had within her the spiritual stone, our Savior: 'The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner'; and: 'A stone was cut from the mountain without hands,' and wrapped, because of our old errors, in good hope. But he was also crucified for the redemption of our sins: then your soul is cleansed from adultery, fornications, drunkenness, and the rest, and then you carry the heavenly word within, as in your own hands; this is what Isaiah said: 'From fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived, and we have brought forth the spirit of your salvation, which you have made upon the earth.' Indeed the Old Testament had the Savior in its service; for the Savior was hidden from the false Hebrews, but he appeared to us.
Well then was it said of the vulture and the stone.

With this stone David slew Goliath; with two stones Aaron and Hur supported the hands of Moses, and put Amalek to flight. The vulture has no single dwelling nor lair; and we too followed the old idolatry (that is, the worship of idols and of many gods), having no dwelling, until faith appeared in the Church, whence the heavenly, fatherly grace appeared; and then we were saved through Jesus Christ.

div.head: On the Ant-lion
div.p: In Job, Eliphaz the king of the Temanites said of the ant-lion: 'It perishes because it has no food.'

Its father has the face of a lion, and eats flesh; its mother has the face of an ant, and eats vegetables. When she has given birth to the ant-lion, having two natures, it perishes: the face of a lion, but the front and back parts of an ant; it cannot eat flesh, because of its mother's nature, nor vegetables, because of its father's nature: it goes therefore to its ruin, because it has no food.

So too is every man of double heart, unstable in all his ways. It is not fitting to walk two ways, foolish and double, with idle hands, and a sinner going two ways; as it is written in wisdom: 'Let your yes be yes, your no, no.'

div.head: On the Weasel
div.p: The law says: 'You shall not eat the weasel, nor anything like it.'

The weasel has this nature: it receives the male's seed in its mouth, and, becoming pregnant, gives birth through its ears. If it happens through the right ear, it will be a male; if through the left, a female. Evil things, then, are generated from the ears.

There are, then, even now those who eat the spiritual and heavenly bread in the church; but when they are dismissed, they cast the word out of their ears, and become as it is said in the fifty-seventh psalm: 'Like the deaf asp that stops her ears, which will not hear the voice of the charmer, or the sorcerer who is skillfully charmed.'

div.head: On the Unicorn
div.p: Moses spoke of the unicorn in Deuteronomy, blessing Joseph: 'His glory is like the firstborn of a bull, his horns are like the horns of the unicorn.'

The monoceros, that is the unicorn, has this nature: it is a small animal, like a kid, exceedingly fierce, and has one horn in the middle of its head. No hunter can approach it, because it is extremely strong. How then is it hunted? They place a chaste virgin before it; it leaps into the virgin's lap, and she warms it, and nourishes that animal; and it is taken to the palace of kings.

It has one horn, because the Savior said: 'I and the Father are one.' For he raised up for us a horn of salvation, in the house of David his servant; coming from heaven, he came into the womb of the Virgin Mary: 'Beloved, as the son of unicorns,' as David says in the psalm.

div.head: On the Beaver
div.p: There is an animal called the beaver, exceedingly innocent and quiet. Its testicles are useful for medicine; it is found in the palace of the king. The hunter runs to catch it in the mountains; and the beaver, seeing the pursuing hunter, bites off its own testicles with its mouth, and gives them, throwing them to the hunter. But if another hunter should later pursue it, it throws itself on its back, and shows itself to the hunter; and the hunter, seeing that it has no testicles, departs from it.

O you too, who act manfully, citizen of God, if you give the hunter what belongs to him, he will not come near you again; that is, if you have evil desire, covetousness, adultery, theft, cut these off from yourself, and give them to the devil. So the Apostle also said: 'Render to all their dues; tribute to whom tribute is due, honor to whom honor is due,' and so on. First let us cast away the base sins that are in us to the devil, that is, his works; and so let us give to God the things that are God's, the vows of prayer, the fruit of our good works.

div.head: On the Hyena
div.p: The law said: 'You shall not eat the hyena, nor anything like it.'
It is arsenothelys, that is, male-female; sometimes it becomes male, sometimes female: it is an unclean animal, because it has two natures;

and so Jeremiah too said: 'Is my heritage to me like the den of a hyena?' So too every man of double mind is compared to the hyena: as a sign, they gather to themselves something of the male, that is, of the mind; but when the assembly is dismissed, they take on a womanly nature.
Well did the Physiologus speak.

div.head: On the Nile-Creature
div.p: There is an animal called the nile-creature, dwelling in the river, having the shape of a dog. It is an enemy to the crocodile; if it sees the crocodile sleeping, with its mouth open, the nile-creature goes and smears itself entirely with mud; and when the mud has dried, it leaps into the crocodile's mouth, and casts out all its intestines and inward parts.

So too is the unintelligible hell, seizing every soul and putting it to death: but our heavenly Savior, taking an earthly body, went down into hell, until he might snatch away and lead out those who had died before, according to the holy promises, and that the strength and sting of death might be loosed.

div.head: On the Echineumon
div.p: There is an animal called the echineumon, an enemy to the dragon. If it finds the dragon, it goes against it and smears itself with mud, and covers its nostrils with its tail, hiding and puffing itself up, and so stands against the dragon, until it kills it.

So too our Savior, taking the substance of an earthly body, that is, the body he took from Mary, stood firm until he slew the intelligible dragon, Pharaoh, who sits over the rivers of Egypt, that is, the devil.

div.head: On the Crow
div.p: The prophet Jeremiah testifies: 'You sat like a solitary crow in the wilderness.'
The Physiologus declared that it belongs to one mate; and if the male dies, she does not join with another male, nor does the body of the male mix with another female.

So now the solitary crow is the synagogue of the Jews, the earthly Jerusalem, which killed her heavenly husband, for which reason she is desolate, having no husband, Christ. For the Apostle said of those who believed from among the Gentiles: 'I have espoused you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.' We have then a husband, the divine word, in our souls, so that no stranger may come near, and we be found a den of thieves.

div.head: On the Turtledove
div.p: Solomon said: 'The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.'
The turtledove dwells in the wilderness, that is, withdrawing into solitary places; it does not love to be in the midst of many.

And our Savior himself dwelt on the Mount of Olives (as it is said); taking Peter, James, and John, Jesus went up into the mountain. The turtledove loves to withdraw in silence: so too noble Christ-bearers choose to dwell in secret; they are called Christ-bearers because they are clothed in Christ, imitating the turtledove, our Lord Christ.

div.head: On the Swallow
div.p: King Hezekiah said in the prophet Isaiah: 'Like a swallow, so will I cry, and like a dove I will mourn.' And in Jeremiah it is said: 'The turtledove and the swallow and the stork observed the time of their coming.'
The Physiologus spoke of the swallow, that it gives birth once, and no more.
My Savior too was born once in the womb; he was borne once, was crucified once, and rose from the dead once: 'One God, one faith, one baptism.'

div.head: On the Stag
div.p: In the forty-first psalm it says: 'As the stag desires the springs of water, so my soul desires you, O God.'

The stag is an enemy to the dragon; the dragon flees from the stag into the cracks of the earth; and the stag goes and, having drunk, fills its nostrils with water from the spring, and pours it out into the crack in the earth, and draws out the dragon, and tramples it, and kills it.

So too our Lord slew the great dragon, the devil, with heavenly waters, of which he had ineffable wisdom; for the dragon cannot bear water, nor can the devil bear heavenly words. If you too have intelligible dragons hidden in your heart, call upon Christ through the Gospels, by prayers, and he himself will kill it: for you are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you.

Where the hair of a stag appears in a house, or is burned from its bones, you will never find a dragon there: if the footprint of God and the fear of Christ are found in your heart, no unclean spirit will enter into you.

div.head: On the Frog
div.p: There is a frog called cerseus, that is, the dry-loving one. This dry frog does not mind the heat through the summer; but if the rain overtakes it, it dies; but the other, water-loving frogs that are among the waters, if they see the sun's rays and grow warm, plunge themselves into the spring.

This means the noble abstainers, who are dry-loving. It does not concern them, who labor patiently in abstinence; but if rain overtakes them, they die (that is, the desires of the world); but the water-frogs among them are those who do not endure abstinence. And if they abstain for a day, not bearing the intelligible ray of the sun, they plunge themselves again into their former desires.

This is a marvelous thing in Daniel, of the three brothers: they were thrown into the furnace of fire, that they might sing a hymn to God. Truly it is not marvelous, for they were righteous; and if the righteous raised their dead, it is no great thing that mountains should be moved into the sea.

div.head: On the Lizard, that is the Salamander
div.p: The Physiologus spoke of the lizard called the salamander, that if it enters into a furnace of fire or a bath's oven, every fire is extinguished;
such is its nature. How much better, then, are those who through righteousness extinguished the power of fire, and stopped the mouths of lions.

div.head: On the Magnet Stone
div.p: There is a stone called the magnet, which lifts iron, if it clings to iron -- that is, if it is applied to iron.
If then a creature does this, how much more does the Creator and Maker of all things suspend the sky above the earth, and stretch out the heavens like a skin.

div.head: On the Adamant Stone
div.p: There is an adamant stone, found in the regions of the East, not shining by day in the sunlight, but found by night; it is called adamant because it masters all things, and no one can master it.

My Lord and Savior judges all, and is judged by no one. And in the prophet Amos it says: 'And I saw an adamant stone.' And you, if you are found in the regions of the East, especially if you are called just, blameless, and pious, like Job, innocent, and so on, from the rising of the sun.

div.head: On the Doves
div.p: John the Evangelist says: 'I saw heaven opened, and the Spirit of God descending like a dove upon him.'

The Physiologus spoke of many doves; there are decoy-doves; for there are many kinds of doves, of many and varied colors: there is the black, the ash-grey, one having the color of gold, the honey-colored (that is, dark), the speckled, the white, the red; and if all these doves were sent to the fowlers, none would lure the others in, only the red one would lure and calm them all.

So too the blood of my Savior led all into eternal life: not Moses, because he gave the law, not Isaiah, nor any of the prophets, but the Son of God himself, coming, our Lord Jesus Christ, saved us by his holy blood. This same thing happened for the harlot: because of the scarlet sign her soul was saved: Rahab received the scarlet purple by lot. And in the Song of Songs it says: 'Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your speech is beautiful.' And in Matthew: 'They put a scarlet robe on him.'

div.head: On the Sun-Lizard, that is the Sun-Eel
div.p: There is one called the sun-lizard, that is, the eel of the sun. When it grows old, it is hindered in both its eyes, and grows blind, not seeing the light of the sun. What will it do? By its own good nature it seeks out a wall facing the east, and enters into a crack in the wall, looking to the east, and as the sun rises, its eyes are opened, and it is made new.

So too you, O man, if you have the garment of the old man, take care lest, when the eyes of your heart are hindered, you seek the intelligible rising sun, the Lord Jesus Christ, whose name is called the Dayspring in the prophet Jeremiah. And he is the sun of righteousness, as the Apostle says; and he will open for you the intelligible eyes of your heart, and a new garment will be made for you in place of the old.
